entries.intent: Describe personality precisely with about fifteen adjectives: conscientious, assertive, impulsive, meticulous, aloof, gregarious, complacent, headstrong.

entries.workingTitle: Positive and negative words for the same trait
entries.intent: Choose between words for the same trait that show approval or criticism, about twelve words in pairs: sensitive or touchy, thrifty or tight-fisted, inquisitive or nosy, self-assured or cocky.

entries.workingTitle: Will for typical behaviour: she'll talk for hours
entries.intent: Describe typical behaviour and make confident guesses with will, and complain with stressed will or would: She'll sit for hours reading. That'll be Sam. He WILL leave his socks on the floor.
Say what people are like with about twelve idioms: set in your ways, down to earth, full of yourself, have a heart of gold, have a short fuse, have a big mouth, wear your heart on your sleeve.

entries.workingTitle: Reading dictionary usage notes on near synonyms
entries.intent: Use the register labels, collocations and usage notes of dictionary entries to choose between near synonyms (error, mistake, slip, oversight) and explain why one fits.

entries.workingTitle: Precise words for how people look
entries.intent: Describe how people look in precise detail with about twelve words: stocky, lanky, petite, slender, scruffy, immaculate, weather-beaten, clean-shaven.
Talk about how people see themselves with about twelve words and phrases: self-awareness, self-image, self-doubt, persona, identity crisis, sense of belonging, comfort zone.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a long magazine profile of a chef
entries.intent: Read a long magazine profile of a celebrated chef and infer the chef's personality from the details the writer chooses to show, rather than from direct description.
Name mixed and precise feelings with about fifteen adjectives: apprehensive, elated, indignant, resentful, nostalgic, ambivalent, exasperated, wistful.
Describe moods vividly with about twelve idioms: over the moon, on cloud nine, down in the dumps, on edge, at the end of your tether, a bag of nerves.
Read the obituary of a scientist, follow how it tells the story of a life, moving between work and family, and say what its tone suggests about the writer's view of the person.
Describe how people speak and express themselves with about twelve adjectives: blunt, tactful, outspoken, evasive, long-winded, articulate, curt, reticent.
Understand and use about twelve informal British words in relaxed conversation: knackered, gobsmacked, skint, quid, brolly, dodgy, faff, chock-a-block.
Join in friendly teasing among friends and take a joke well: Very funny, You're never going to let me forget that, are you?, I'll take that as a compliment, Says you!

entries.workingTitle: Reading an old friend's email full of in-jokes
entries.intent: Read a long email from an old friend full of in-jokes, teasing and references to shared memories, and work out the real news and the feelings that the humour carries or hides.
Be deliberately approximate in speech with about twelve expressions: or so, give or take, or thereabouts, the best part of, upwards of, getting on for, and whatnot.

entries.workingTitle: Reading an article on British regional dialects
entries.intent: Read an article on regional dialects in Britain and identify the features it describes (words, grammar, pronunciation) and the attitudes to them, including the writer's own.
Show your attitude to what you say with about twelve markers: admittedly, frankly, needless to say, if anything, as it happens, understandably, ironically, to be fair.
Use about fifteen binomials in their fixed order: pros and cons, odds and ends, safe and sound, peace and quiet, ups and downs, wear and tear, sick and tired.
Make descriptions vivid with about twelve fixed similes: as light as a feather, sleep like a log, as good as gold, as cool as a cucumber, as clear as mud, like clockwork.

Voice strong disagreement with a committee's plan without causing offence: I have serious reservations about this, With respect, I think we're overlooking..., I'm not sure that's the best way forward.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a sarcastic forum thread about grammar
entries.intent: Read a forum thread in which posters argue with sarcasm over a usage rule (split infinitives, less or fewer) and tell each poster's real position from what they literally write.
Describe how relationships work and change with about twelve words: rapport, chemistry, mutual respect, bond, tension, strained, rift, estrangement, close-knit.
Talk about love and couples with about twelve idioms: head over heels, love at first sight, an item, a match made in heaven, pop the question, tie the knot, on the rocks.

entries.workingTitle: Reading an opinion piece on online friendship
entries.intent: Read an opinion piece claiming that social media weakens friendship and identify how the writer handles each counter-argument: conceding it, dismissing it or ignoring it.
Persuade people, or give way to them, with about twelve phrasal verbs: talk into, talk out of, win over, bring round, push for, go along with, back down.
Ask for a big favour in a way that makes it easy to refuse: I hate to ask, but..., I wouldn't ask if it weren't important, Feel free to say no, No pressure at all.

entries.workingTitle: Unreal past: it's time we left, I'd rather you didn't
entries.intent: Use a past tense with present meaning after it's (high) time, would rather + subject, and as if or as though: It's time we left. I'd rather you didn't smoke. He talks as if he knew everything.
Talk about disputes and how they end with about twelve words: feud, grievance, bad blood, flashpoint, stalemate, defuse, mediator, reconciliation, extend an olive branch.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a sociology article on the decline of clubs
entries.intent: Read a sociology article on why fewer people join clubs and societies, and tell the survey data from the writer's explanation of it, noting other readings the figures allow.
Strengthen adjectives with the adverb that naturally goes with them, about twelve pairs: deeply concerned, highly unlikely, bitterly disappointed, fully aware, painfully slow.
Smooth over an awkward moment after a social blunder, yours or someone else's: I'm sure no offence was meant, Let's just forget it, Well, moving swiftly on..., I could have put that better.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a psychologist's article on laughter
entries.intent: Read a psychologist's article on why we laugh, follow the argument and how each example supports it, and identify the writer's attitude to rival theories.
Describe how a home is designed and furnished with about twelve words: minimalist, open-plan, period features, feature wall, fixtures and fittings, statement piece, clutter-free.
Say what things are made of and how they look with about twelve words: marble, granite, oak, brass, stainless steel, laminate, glossy, matt, polished.
Read a magazine feature on the redesign of a Victorian terraced house and follow the description of space, light and materials and the designer's reasons for each choice.
Describe the noises of a house with about twelve verbs: creak, rattle, hum, buzz, whirr, gurgle, drip, slam, squeak, tick.
Build and understand words with -ish, -wise, -ward, -proof, -friendly and -fold: fortyish, money-wise, homeward, soundproof, family-friendly, tenfold.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a tense email chain between neighbours
entries.intent: Read an email chain between neighbours about a shared garden and trace the growing irritation behind the polite phrases (as I mentioned before, just to be clear, with respect).
Use about ten idioms built on home: make yourself at home, a home from home, hit home, home and dry, close to home, nothing to write home about, home truths.
Help neighbours in a dispute find what each could give up: What would it take for you to...?, Would you be open to...?, If he agreed to..., could you...?, That sounds like a fair compromise.
Talk about looking after a garden with about twelve words: perennial, seedling, cutting, prune, weed, fertiliser, bloom, wilt, greenhouse, allotment.

entries.workingTitle: Compound adjectives for things and ideas
entries.intent: Describe tasks, products and ideas with about twelve compound adjectives: time-consuming, far-reaching, thought-provoking, long-lasting, labour-saving, eye-catching.
Talk about how people work together today with about twelve words: work-life balance, flexitime, remote working, hot-desking, office politics, presenteeism, team-building.

entries.workingTitle: Reading an article on a four-day week trial
entries.intent: Read a long article on a four-day working week trial and separate the trial's actual results from what supporters and critics claim those results prove.
Talk about building a career with about twelve words: career path, mentor, appraisal, transferable skills, job shadowing, sabbatical, career break, freelance, headhunt.
Talk about time and timing with about ten idioms: in the nick of time, against the clock, a race against time, once in a blue moon, kill time, behind the times.
Make contacts at a conference, say briefly what you do and offer introductions: We specialise in..., You might want to talk to..., I'd be happy to put you in touch with..., Mind if I drop you a line?
Use about twelve idioms common at work: get the ball rolling, cut corners, think outside the box, back to square one, call it a day, a ballpark figure, the bottom line.

entries.workingTitle: Cleft sentences: it was Anna who, what I need is
entries.intent: Focus on one part of a sentence with it is or it was + focus + who or that, and with what + clause + be: It was Anna who called, not Tom. What I need is a holiday.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a long article on the gig economy
entries.intent: Read a long-form article on the gig economy and assess how the writer combines personal stories with statistics, and whether that evidence really supports the conclusion.
Read and use about fifteen abbreviations from emails, notes and forms, including two that people confuse: i.e. and e.g., NB, cf., FYI, encl., c/o, approx., TBC, ETA, PTO, RSVP, w/c.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a personal essay on a career change
entries.intent: Read a personal essay about changing career at forty and see how the writer turns personal anecdotes into a general argument the reader can accept or reject.
Negotiate pay or contract terms, trading concessions without losing goodwill: I was hoping for something closer to..., Is there any flexibility on...?, I could accept that if...
Say how music sounds and feels with about twelve words: catchy, haunting, upbeat, mellow, soulful, infectious, discordant, harmony, tempo, acoustic.
Talk about how a play is staged and received with about twelve words: playwright, rehearsal, dress rehearsal, understudy, props, opening night, matinee, curtain call, standing ovation.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a scene from a modern play
entries.intent: Read a scene from a modern play and work out the subtext: what the characters want, feel or hide behind what they actually say to each other.
Talk about how films are made with about twelve words: screenplay, cinematography, footage, editing, close-up, on location, stunt double, dubbed, subtitled.
Talk about art today and how it is shown with about twelve words: installation, conceptual art, street art, mixed media, canvas, curator, retrospective, provocative.
Discuss who pays for culture and who it is for with about twelve words: patron, subsidy, arts grant, arts council, highbrow, lowbrow, mainstream, elitist.
Read a curator's essay in an exhibition catalogue and separate the description of the works from the curator's interpretation and the claims made for the artist.
Describe how people lead and manage teams with about twelve words: delegate, oversee, accountable, empower, micromanage, hands-off, chain of command, morale.
Name the parts and procedures of a formal meeting with about twelve words: agenda, minutes, quorum, consensus, unanimous, a show of hands, adjourn, action points, any other business.
Open a meeting, move through the agenda, keep to time and close each item: Shall we make a start?, Let's move on to item three, I'm conscious of the time, Can we agree on that?

entries.workingTitle: Reading meeting minutes between the lines
entries.intent: Read the minutes of a staff meeting and find the decisions, the actions and who owns them, and the disagreement hidden in neutral wording (concerns were raised, it was noted).

entries.workingTitle: The subjunctive after suggest and insist
entries.intent: Follow suggest, insist and it is vital that with should + verb, the formal bare subjunctive or, in British English, the present simple: I suggest that he should apply, he apply or he applies.
Describe work tasks in formal English with about twelve verbs: implement, facilitate, allocate, liaise, prioritise, coordinate, consolidate, expedite, undertake.

entries.workingTitle: Phrasal verbs for ideas and impressions
entries.intent: Talk about understanding and coming across with about twelve phrasal verbs: come across as, get across, take in, sink in, make out, come down to, boil down to, catch on.
Write a reference for a former colleague or student: I have known Maya for three years, She consistently..., I have no hesitation in recommending her for...

entries.workingTitle: Reading between the lines of a job reference
entries.intent: Read a reference for a job applicant and find what it praises, what it carefully leaves out and what faint praise (always punctual, a pleasant colleague) tells the employer.
Recognise and use about twelve polite ways of saying awkward things: between jobs, let someone go, economical with the truth, senior citizens, of a certain age, use the facilities.
Talk about spending and saving with about ten idioms: tighten your belt, save for a rainy day, in the red, a nest egg, money to burn, foot the bill, pay your way.
Discuss the state of the economy with about twelve words: recession, downturn, recovery, boom, slump, inflation, GDP, living standards, consumer spending.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a restructuring memo for euphemisms
entries.intent: Read an internal memo announcing a restructuring and translate its euphemisms (streamlining, a leaner structure, new opportunities) into what will actually happen to staff.
Discuss how companies grow and compete with about twelve words: merger, takeover, acquisition, stakeholder, revenue, turnover, market share, diversify, outsource.
Give disappointing news to a colleague tactfully and handle their reaction: I'm afraid I have some bad news, Unfortunately, the board has decided..., I know this isn't what you were hoping for.
Describe how figures change with about twelve verbs and adverbs: soar, plummet, surge, dip, fluctuate, peak, level off, plateau, considerably, steeply, dramatically.

entries.workingTitle: Reading financial news on a retailer's results
entries.intent: Read a news report on a retailer's annual results and work out what the main figures (sales, profit, margins) mean and how different analysts interpret them.
Talk about investing money with about twelve words: shares, the stock market, stockbroker, investor, dividend, portfolio, bonds, return on investment, high-risk.
Talk about saving for later life with about twelve words: state pension, workplace pension, contributions, lump sum, annuity, compound interest, ISA, retirement age.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a personal finance column on mortgages
entries.intent: Read a newspaper column on choosing a mortgage and identify each piece of advice and the conditions under which the columnist says it holds (fixed or variable, long or short term).
Name the tools writers use with about twelve words: metaphor, simile, imagery, irony, symbolism, foreshadowing, flashback, personification, motif.

entries.workingTitle: Reading an extract from a contemporary novel
entries.intent: Read an extract from a contemporary novel and infer the characters' motives and the narrator's point of view from dialogue, gesture and detail.
Talk about how books reach readers with about twelve words: publisher, manuscript, edition, royalties, ghostwriter, blurb, page-turner, out of print, self-publish.
Read a short contemporary poem, follow how the speaker's attitude shifts from the first lines to the last and describe the tone at each stage.

entries.workingTitle: Inversion: never have I seen, little did she know
entries.intent: Add emphasis in formal style by putting never, rarely, seldom, little, hardly, no sooner, not only or under no circumstances first and inverting: Never have I seen such a mess. Little did she know.
Praise or criticise a book, film or show with about twelve collocations: critically acclaimed, highly recommended, a compelling read, fall flat, wooden acting, a lacklustre performance.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a review that compares two books
entries.intent: Read a review comparing two non-fiction books on the same subject and follow how the reviewer weighs one against the other, which one wins and on what grounds.

entries.workingTitle: Building on what others have said
entries.intent: Link your contribution to earlier points in a book club discussion: Picking up on what Sam said..., To build on that..., That ties in with..., I'd go even further than Ana and say...

entries.workingTitle: Reading a short story with an open ending
entries.intent: Read a literary short story that ends without resolution and argue for one interpretation of the ending, using clues from earlier in the text.
Talk about how products are marketed with about twelve words: market research, target market, niche market, brand image, brand loyalty, rebrand, endorsement, word of mouth.
Recognise about twelve words and phrases adverts use to persuade: limited edition, exclusive offer, while stocks last, unbeatable, hassle-free, new and improved, award-winning.

entries.workingTitle: Reading advertising copy for misleading claims
entries.intent: Read adverts for skincare products and explain how their claims mislead without lying (up to, helps reduce, clinically tested, nine out of ten women agreed).
Describe clothes and personal style with about twelve words: chic, elegant, flattering, tailored, figure-hugging, oversized, vintage, timeless, effortless.
Place products on the scale from cheap to luxurious with about twelve words: no-frills, budget, bargain-basement, mass-market, mid-range, upmarket, high-end, premium.
Know your legal rights as a buyer with about twelve words: terms and conditions, statutory rights, small claims court, cooling-off period, liable, breach of contract, chargeback.
Probe and rephrase your questions until a salesperson or a supplier gives a clear answer: So what you're telling me is..., Let me put it another way, Is that a yes or a no?

entries.workingTitle: Reading an evasive reply to a complaint
entries.intent: Read a company's carefully worded answer to a formal complaint and separate firm commitments from hedges and non-promises (we will look into, where possible, at our discretion).
Discuss buying with a conscience with about twelve words: fair trade, ethical sourcing, cruelty-free, sweatshop, child labour, greenwashing, shop local, conscious consumer.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a consumer investigation into hidden fees
entries.intent: Read a consumer magazine's investigation into hidden booking fees and compare what it found with the explanations the companies gave in response.
Use about twelve computing words with their everyday meanings: a glitch, by default, bandwidth (time and energy), take it offline, ping someone, a workaround.
Discuss how technology changes society with about twelve words: automation, algorithm, big data, disruption, digital divide, digital literacy, digital native, tech giant.
Coordinate a remote team project in writing, giving instructions and weighing up proposals: Could everyone send their sections by Friday?, I've left some comments, I'd lean towards option two.
Talk about keeping data and devices safe with about twelve words: malware, ransomware, spyware, encryption, firewall, data breach, two-factor authentication, identity theft.
Read an app's privacy policy and find, through its vague wording, what data is collected, who it is shared with, how long it is kept and how to opt out.

entries.workingTitle: Relative clauses: some of which, all of whom, whereby
entries.intent: Add information formally with a quantifier + of which or of whom, and with whereby: She has three sons, all of whom are doctors. It's a system whereby members pay monthly.
Talk about how public places are kept secure with about twelve words: CCTV, surveillance, patrol, crackdown, metal detector, bag search, ID badge, security clearance.

entries.workingTitle: Reading an article on smart homes and privacy
entries.intent: Read an article on smart home devices and weigh the benefits it describes against the privacy risks it raises, then identify where the writer finally stands.

entries.workingTitle: Nouns as verbs, verbs as nouns
entries.intent: Use about twelve words that change class with no suffix (conversion): to google, to bin, to head a team, to shoulder the blame, to pocket, a must, a good buy, a rethink.
Describe how devices and systems work with about twelve technical words: specification, component, mechanism, interface, output, compatible, configure, calibrate, malfunction.
Discuss advances in science and technology with about twelve words: cutting-edge, stem cells, gene therapy, cloning, nanotechnology, robotics, quantum computing, 3D printing.
Read a technology firm's white paper on a home battery and separate measurable specifications from marketing claims that the reader has no way to check.
Describe holiday places as a travel writer would with about twelve adjectives: breathtaking, unspoilt, secluded, idyllic, tranquil, quaint, far-flung, tucked away.
Talk about travel with about ten idioms: hit the road, travel light, get itchy feet, live out of a suitcase, catch the travel bug, a whistle-stop tour, the open road.
Read a magazine feature about a remote Scottish island, spot the signs that a sponsor paid for the trip and judge how that shapes the praise and what is left out.
Understand about twelve formal words and phrases from travel announcements and notices: depart, commence boarding, alight, disembark, terminate, onward journey, calling at.
Talk about planning and changing a route with about twelve words: detour, stopover, layover (US), en route, in transit, the scenic route, a leg of the journey, a short cut.

Take a complaint about a rail company or an airline further when the first answer is not good enough: I'd like to escalate this, This is the third time I've raised it, Unless this is resolved, I'll...

entries.workingTitle: Reading a hotel's replies to bad reviews
entries.intent: Read guests' negative reviews of a hotel and the manager's public replies, and judge which replies calm the complaint and which sound defensive, sarcastic or insincere.

entries.workingTitle: Inverted conditionals: had I known, should you need
entries.intent: Write formal conditions without if by inverting had, should and were: Had I known, I would have called. Should you need help, ask at reception. Were she to resign, who would replace her?
Talk about roads, rail and the networks around them with about twelve words: bypass, ring road, flyover, underpass, toll road, viaduct, slip road, level crossing, bottleneck.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a rail accident investigation report
entries.intent: Read the summary of a rail accident investigation and follow the chain of causes, from the immediate cause to the underlying ones, and the recommendations made.
Talk about new ways of getting around with about twelve words: electric vehicle, hybrid, charging point, range anxiety, e-scooter, e-bike, car club, ride-hailing, self-driving car.
Discuss the impact of tourism and how to reduce it with about twelve words: mass tourism, carbon offsetting, ecotourism, responsible travel, slow travel, flight shame, local economy.

entries.workingTitle: Reading an essay in praise of slow travel
entries.intent: Read an essay arguing for slow travel by train and boat, identify the values behind the argument and the objections the writer anticipates and answers.
Talk about moving to and settling in another country with about twelve words: expat, relocate, emigrate, culture shock, adjust, settle in, put down roots, host country.

entries.workingTitle: Reading visa rules and their exceptions
entries.intent: Read an official page of visa rules for working abroad and work out which conditions apply to which applicant, where the exceptions lie and which documents each case needs.
Avoid mistakes with about twelve English words that look like words in other languages but mean something else: actual, eventual, sympathetic, embarrassed, pretend, attend, deception, fabric.
Interpret informally between colleagues, giving the sense rather than every word and explaining cultural references: Roughly, she's saying..., There's no direct equivalent, but..., It's a bit like...
Discuss a connected world with about twelve words: free movement, multinational, global supply chain, interdependence, emerging economies, cultural exchange, homogenisation.
Discuss nations and belonging with about twelve words: separatism, national pride, patriotism, nationalism, regional identity, national anthem, independence movement.
Read an extract from a memoir about moving to Britain as a child and infer the writer's feelings about identity and belonging from what is shown rather than stated.
Follow the British university application process with about twelve words: UCAS, foundation year, entry requirements, predicted grades, conditional offer, clearing, deferred entry.
Discuss how schools are run and judged in England with about twelve words: national curriculum, league tables, Ofsted, academy, free school, special educational needs, inclusive education.

entries.workingTitle: Reading the guidelines for a scholarship
entries.intent: Read the guidelines for a postgraduate scholarship and decide who is eligible, how applications are scored and which conditions an applicant could easily miss.
Discuss how memory and attention work with about twelve words: cognitive, neuroscience, short-term memory, long-term memory, retention, recall, concentration, attention span.
Write a personal statement for a university or job application: What first drew me to this subject was..., Having worked as..., I am particularly keen to..., I believe I would bring...
Describe what research and academic writing do with about fifteen verbs: analyse, assess, evaluate, examine, interpret, outline, demonstrate, indicate, illustrate.
Write formally by turning clauses into noun phrases (they arrived late becomes their late arrival) and refer back with summary nouns (this decision) and with the former and the latter.

entries.workingTitle: Reading an article on language and thought
entries.intent: Read an article on whether the language we speak shapes how we think, and weigh the evidence it offers for the strong and the weak versions of the idea.
Discuss ideas in academic English with about fifteen nouns: approach, concept, framework, perspective, factor, criterion, phenomenon, dimension, scope, significance.

entries.workingTitle: Verb and noun collocations in formal writing
entries.intent: Use about twelve verb and noun collocations of formal writing: raise concerns, pose a threat, address an issue, draw a conclusion, conduct research, meet the criteria, gain insight.
Ask open questions that push a group to think further and build on their answers: What makes you say that?, How does that fit with...?, What would happen if...?, Is that always true?
Describe flavours precisely with about twelve adjectives: tangy, zesty, rich, aromatic, savoury, smoky, earthy, subtle, overpowering.
Talk about top-end restaurants with about twelve words: gourmet, delicacy, tasting menu, signature dish, Michelin-starred, sommelier, wine pairing, palate.
Read a restaurant review packed with jokes and wordplay and work out the critic's real verdict on the food, the service and the value for money behind the humour.
Use about twelve idioms built on food: a piece of cake, not my cup of tea, the icing on the cake, take something with a pinch of salt, spill the beans, sell like hot cakes.

entries.workingTitle: Reading an essay on a regional food culture
entries.intent: Read a food writer's essay on the cooking of one region and see how description, memory and argument combine to make the case for its value.
Talk about formal meals and table manners with about twelve words: black tie, place setting, seating plan, dress code, guest of honour, say grace, second helping.
Discuss what food does in the body with about twelve words: metabolism, digestion, gut health, fibre, saturated fat, antioxidant, micronutrients, blood sugar, deficiency.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a business proposal for a café
entries.intent: Read a proposal to open a second branch of a café and assess the case it makes: the costs, the expected income, the risks it admits and the ones it plays down.
Grant part of an opposing argument while standing your ground, in a debate about eating meat: I'll grant you that..., That's a fair point, but it doesn't change the fact that..., True, but...
Discuss whether the world can feed itself with about twelve words: food prices, food shortage, famine, malnutrition, crop failure, staple crop, food bank, food aid.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a report on a food labelling scandal
entries.intent: Read a report on a meat mislabelling scandal and trace how the problem spread along the supply chain and whom the writer holds responsible, and why.
Deal with water, gas and electricity services with about twelve words: supplier, unit rate, standing charge, meter reading, switch supplier, power cut, the National Grid, hosepipe ban.
Talk about dealing with officials and forms with about twelve words: red tape, paperwork, bureaucrat, form-filling, backlog, processing time, rubber-stamp, jump through hoops.

entries.workingTitle: Setting the record straight in writing
entries.intent: Write to an organisation to correct a misunderstanding or a mistake about you: I would like to clarify that..., Contrary to what your letter states..., I trust this resolves the matter.
Understand about twelve words from everyday legal documents: will, executor, probate, deed, clause, power of attorney, witness a signature, legal guardian.

entries.workingTitle: Reading contract clauses on liability and termination
entries.intent: Read clauses from a business service contract on liability and ending the agreement and work out who is responsible for what, under which conditions and with which exceptions.
Discuss taxes and government spending with about twelve words: income tax, VAT, National Insurance, tax return, tax bracket, loophole, public spending, budget deficit.

entries.workingTitle: Reading tax guidance for the self-employed
entries.intent: Read official tax guidance for sole traders and find which expenses can be claimed, under what conditions, and which missed deadlines lead to a penalty.

entries.workingTitle: Participle clauses: not knowing, being asked, with prices rising
entries.intent: Use past participle clauses, not + -ing, being + past participle and with + object + -ing: Built in 1900, the hall needs work. Not knowing what to say, I left. With prices rising, people spend less.
Replace about twelve everyday phrasal verbs with formal verbs: put off and postpone, find out and discover, carry on and continue, set up and establish, put up with and tolerate.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a plain English style guide
entries.intent: Read a guide to plain English and use its principles (short sentences, active verbs, everyday words) to judge which version of an official letter works best and why.

entries.workingTitle: Explaining a document in plain words
entries.intent: Explain a document such as a contract clause or an official letter to a relative who has not read it: This part says that..., Put simply..., What it doesn't say is..., The bit to watch out for is...

entries.workingTitle: Reading a letter rejecting an insurance claim
entries.intent: Read an insurer's letter turning down a claim and identify the grounds given, the policy terms quoted and the steps and deadline for challenging the decision.
Name health professionals by speciality and talk about being referred, with about twelve words: consultant, cardiologist, dermatologist, paediatrician, anaesthetist, oncologist, midwife, referral.
Understand what doctors say about an illness with about twelve words: diagnose, misdiagnose, prognosis, chronic, acute, terminal, remission, relapse, underlying condition.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a consent form for a medical procedure
entries.intent: Read a patient information and consent form for a minor operation and find the risks, the alternatives, the recovery time and exactly what you agree to by signing.
Talk about feeling ill and getting better with about ten idioms: under the weather, off colour, run-down, on the mend, back on your feet, fighting fit, a clean bill of health.

entries.workingTitle: May well, might well, might as well
entries.intent: Say something is quite likely with may well, might well or could well, and that there is no better option with might as well or may as well: It may well rain. We might as well go home.

entries.workingTitle: Speaking up for a relative at the doctor's
entries.intent: Speak up for an elderly relative at a medical appointment and make sure their concerns are heard: I'm not sure my mother fully understood, Could you explain why...?, We'd like a second opinion.
Talk about mental illness and getting help with about twelve words: depression, panic attack, eating disorder, mental health crisis, stigma, counselling, talking therapy, mindfulness.

entries.workingTitle: Reading an article on burnout at work
entries.intent: Read a long article on burnout and separate the research it cites from the writer's interpretation and the advice it gives, judging how well each is supported.
Discuss treatments outside mainstream medicine with about twelve words: acupuncture, homeopathy, herbal remedy, aromatherapy, chiropractor, holistic, complementary, unproven.
Discuss health across a population with about twelve words: outbreak, epidemic, pandemic, contagious, quarantine, self-isolate, screening, herd immunity, life expectancy.
Read leaflets and posters from a campaign to cut drinking and identify the audience each one targets and how it persuades: fear, humour, statistics or social pressure.
Talk about growing old and needing support with about twelve words: frail, dementia, memory loss, carer, home help, respite care, sheltered housing, independent living.
Understand how social services protect people with about twelve words: social worker, caseworker, safeguarding, child protection, foster care, in care, vulnerable adult, care package.
Write a sympathy card or a longer letter after a death: I was so sorry to hear about..., He will be greatly missed, I have such happy memories of..., Please don't hesitate to call.
Talk about how television and radio are run with about twelve words: broadcaster, public service broadcasting, licence fee, prime time, the watershed, ratings, coverage, bias.
Discuss money and rules in professional sport with about twelve words: sponsorship, broadcasting rights, transfer fee, prize money, governing body, doping, match-fixing, ban.
Use about twelve idioms from sport at work and in daily life: move the goalposts, a level playing field, on the ball, the ball is in your court, par for the course, jump the gun.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a football column full of idiom
entries.intent: Read a football column rich in idiom and metaphor (a game of two halves, parking the bus) and pin down what the columnist actually thinks of the team and its manager.
Talk about new ways of spending free time with about twelve words: forest bathing, glamping, wellness, digital detox, wild swimming, escape room, bucket list, hobbyist.
Give a long interview about your life or work, developing your answers and returning to your point after interruptions: That's a complicated question, If I could go back to what you asked earlier...
Talk about training and physical ability with about twelve words: stamina, endurance, agility, flexibility, posture, core strength, pull a muscle, recovery time, overtraining.
Describe natural scenery vividly with about twelve words and phrases: rolling hills, jagged peaks, sheer cliffs, a rugged coastline, barren, lush, dense forest, winding.
Put an object first for emphasis, or a complement or a place adverbial first with inversion: That I can't accept. More worrying is the cost. On the hill stood a castle.
Describe how the land is shaped with about twelve words: terrain, altitude, tectonic plates, fault line, erosion, sediment, flood plain, fertile, arid.
Describe light and the sky at different times with about twelve words: dawn, daybreak, dusk, twilight, half-light, haze, glare, gloom, starlit.
Use about ten idioms built on weather: a storm in a teacup, it never rains but it pours, come rain or shine, weather the storm, get wind of, under a cloud.

entries.workingTitle: Reading first-hand accounts of a great storm
entries.intent: Read several eyewitness accounts of a famous storm and compare what each person noticed, felt and remembered, and how time has shaped each story.
Understand how weather is explained and measured with about twelve words: meteorologist, high pressure, low pressure, cold front, warm front, isobar, precipitation, humidity, visibility.

entries.workingTitle: Reading an article on how forecasts are made
entries.intent: Read a science article on weather forecasting and explain how computer models work, what a 70 per cent chance of rain means and why forecasts become less reliable further ahead.
Discuss the science of climate change with about twelve words: climate model, feedback loop, tipping point, permafrost, mitigation, adaptation, carbon neutral, net zero, carbon budget.

entries.workingTitle: Reading an article on the Little Ice Age
entries.intent: Read an article on the Little Ice Age and separate the historical evidence (diaries, frost fairs on the Thames, harvest records) from the scientists' interpretation of it.
Speculate about the climate under different scenarios, past and future: Had we acted sooner..., Should temperatures rise further..., Were the ice sheets to melt faster...

entries.workingTitle: Reading a city's climate adaptation plan
entries.intent: Read a city's plan for adapting to heatwaves and flooding and find the risks it expects, the measures it proposes and how it ranks them by cost and urgency.
Follow news about the aftermath of a disaster with about twelve words: devastation, death toll, displaced, aftermath, relief effort, humanitarian aid, emergency shelter, rebuild.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a long feature with missing paragraphs
entries.intent: Read a long feature about a town rebuilt after a flood and put its missing paragraphs back, using reference words, linking phrases and the flow of ideas.
Explain how living things depend on each other with about twelve words: keystone species, food chain, food web, predator, pollinator, native species, invasive species, habitat loss.
Discuss how governments protect nature with about twelve words: sustainability, biodiversity, deforestation, overfishing, environmental impact, green taxes, the polluter pays principle.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a report on the decline of farmland birds
entries.intent: Read an environmental report on falling numbers of farmland birds and link each finding to the causes it proposes and the recommendations it makes.
Guide listeners through a long talk on a local conservation project with clear signposts: I've divided my talk into three parts, I'll return to this point later, That brings me to...
Discuss how animals are treated with about twelve words: animal rights, welfare standards, cruelty, neglect, humane, captivity, sanctuary, rescue centre, battery hens, animal testing.
Talk about living with less waste with about twelve words: zero waste, compost, refill, reusable, upcycle, repair café, pre-loved, declutter, make do and mend.
Discuss how towns are planned and renewed with about twelve words: regeneration, green belt, brownfield site, zoning, mixed-use, high-density, new town, pedestrianise.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a local history of a high street
entries.intent: Read a local history of one high street, follow how its shops and people changed over a century and tell the historian's evidence from their nostalgia for what was lost.
Discuss the growth of huge cities with about twelve words: megacity, metropolis, urbanisation, population density, commuter belt, satellite town, shanty town, slum.

entries.workingTitle: No matter what, however hard, whatever
entries.intent: Say that something makes no difference with no matter + wh-word, however + adjective or adverb, and whatever, whoever or wherever: No matter what you say, I'm going. However hard I try, I never win.
Discuss the shortage of homes with about twelve words: affordable housing, social housing, house-building, rent controls, priced out, eviction, rough sleeping, gentrification.
Read a feature on the regeneration of a former docks area and show how the choice and order of quotes from residents, developers and the council reveal the writer's side.
Follow the steps of buying a home and getting permission to build, with about twelve words: surveyor, conveyancing, freehold, leasehold, gazumping, completion, planning permission, listed building.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a planning application and objections
entries.intent: Read a planning application for a home extension and the neighbours' letters of objection, and weigh the arguments on each side against the planning rules quoted.
Deal with residents' questions while presenting a housing plan and keep to your outline: That's actually my next point, I'll come to that in a moment, Could we save questions on cost for the end?
Use about ten idioms built on place and distance: a stone's throw, the middle of nowhere, the back of beyond, all over the place, put somewhere on the map, go places.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a commentary on house prices
entries.intent: Read a commentary forecasting house prices and separate confident predictions from cautious ones, noting what each forecast depends on (interest rates, wages, new building).
Discuss how a democracy works with about twelve words: constituency, MP, cabinet, the opposition, coalition, manifesto, referendum, by-election, legislation.
Talk about politics with about ten idioms: a political football, a hot potato, toe the line, sit on the fence, a U-turn, grass roots, the corridors of power, a lame duck.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a political editorial for hidden assumptions
entries.intent: Read a political editorial and uncover the assumptions it never states and the stance implied by its choice of words, beyond the argument it makes openly.
Discuss wealth and opportunity in society with about twelve words: social mobility, privilege, disadvantaged, marginalised, deprivation, the poverty line, the welfare state, benefits.
Discuss equality between women and men with about twelve words: gender roles, stereotype, sexism, feminism, equal opportunities, glass ceiling, gender pay gap, paternity leave.

entries.workingTitle: Reading the executive summary of a policy report
entries.intent: Read the executive summary of a report on youth unemployment and link each recommendation to the evidence offered for it, noting any that rest on little evidence.
Discuss rights and their abuse with about twelve words: political prisoner, freedom of speech, censorship, the right to privacy, persecution, dissident, asylum, violation.

entries.workingTitle: Prefixes counter-, anti-, pro-, semi-, multi-, inter- and trans-
entries.intent: Build and understand words with counter-, anti-, pro-, semi-, multi-, inter- and trans-: counterproductive, anti-ageing, pro-democracy, semi-retired, interconnected, transatlantic.

entries.workingTitle: Ellipsis and substitution: do so, those of, if necessary
entries.intent: Avoid repetition in formal writing with do so, that of and those of, and short clauses like if so and if necessary: He promised to help and did so. Her salary is double that of her boss.

entries.workingTitle: Spoken markers for building an argument
entries.intent: Add, contrast and sum up points in conversation with about twelve markers: for a start, on top of that, what's more, then again, that said, all the same, at any rate, all in all.

entries.workingTitle: Arguing your case in a formal debate
entries.intent: Argue a formal position in a debate and respond to counter-arguments: My opponent argues that..., That argument overlooks..., Even if we accept that..., it does not follow that...
Read a satirical story written in the style of straight news, recognise that it is satire, name its target and point to the details that give the joke away.
Use about twelve strong adjective and noun collocations: a narrow escape, a heated debate, a vested interest, a sweeping statement, a foregone conclusion, a tall order.
Follow a criminal case with about twelve words: prosecution, defence, defendant, summing-up, testify, cross-examine, hung jury, acquit, convict, appeal, legal aid.
Talk about serious crime and how it is solved with about twelve words: murder, manslaughter, assault, motive, alibi, forensic evidence, organised crime, money laundering.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a summary of a court judgment
entries.intent: Read a published summary of a court judgment and follow the judge's reasoning from the facts found, through the law applied, to the outcome.
Follow news about war and peace with about twelve words: invasion, occupation, troops, air strike, civilian casualties, war crime, ceasefire, truce, treaty, peacekeeping force.
Read a long investigation into how a council awarded its contracts and separate proven facts from allegations, noting how the reporter signals doubt (it is understood, sources claim).
Talk about religious and non-religious views with about twelve words: faith, devout, spiritual, sacred, ritual, pilgrimage, convert, atheist, agnostic, secular.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a guide to a medieval cathedral
entries.intent: Read a visitor guide to a medieval cathedral and follow its tour of the building (nave, choir, cloister) and the reasons it gives for the site's historical importance.
Talk about kings, queens and empires in history with about twelve words: reign, dynasty, heir, throne, coronation, abdicate, succession, the Crown, colony, colonial rule.
Discuss basic philosophical ideas with about twelve words: ethics, morality, logic, reasoning, rational, principle, free will, thought experiment, ideal.
Ask questions that pin down a complex or abstract idea: How would you define...?, Is that the same as...?, Where would you draw the line between...?, Could you give a concrete example?
Raise, support and reject ideas in a discussion with about twelve phrasal verbs: bring up, point out, put forward, back up, rule out, touch on, dwell on, follow up.
Talk about how a study is designed and run with about twelve words: methodology, participant, sample, questionnaire, case study, pilot study, variable, qualitative, quantitative, findings.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a journal abstract and introduction
entries.intent: Read the abstract and introduction of a research article and identify the research question, the gap it claims to fill, the method and the main claim.
Discuss how new treatments are tested with about twelve words: clinical trial, randomised, double-blind, placebo, control group, efficacy, pharmaceutical company, lab results.

entries.workingTitle: Hedging: it would seem, it could be argued
entries.intent: Make claims more cautious with tend to, would seem or appear, and modal passives: Prices tend to rise in winter. It would seem that the plan has failed. It could be argued that it costs too much.
Make academic claims more careful with about twelve adverbs and phrases: arguably, largely, broadly, relatively, potentially, to some extent, in part, in most cases.

entries.workingTitle: Reading the discussion section of a study
entries.intent: Read the discussion section of a research article and tell firm findings from cautious claims (may suggest, appears to) and from the limitations the authors admit.
Restate a speaker's argument in a seminar, check you have it right and test what follows: If I understand you correctly..., Is that a fair summary?, Which would mean..., Doesn't that assume...?
Report what writers claim and show how far you accept it with about twelve verbs: claim, maintain, contend, assert, acknowledge, observe, highlight, challenge, question.

entries.workingTitle: Reading a health news story and the study behind it
entries.intent: Read a news story about diet and heart disease next to the study it reports, and spot where the claims grew stronger or lost their conditions in the retelling.
Acknowledge sources in academic work with about twelve words: cite, citation, quotation, paraphrase, footnote, in-text citation, et al., reference list, bibliography, plagiarism.
Read a university's rules on academic misconduct and sort clear breaches from grey areas (close paraphrase, reusing your own work, AI tools) and the penalty for each.
Connect sentences in formal writing with about twelve linking adverbs: moreover, furthermore, consequently, accordingly, nonetheless, conversely, likewise, notably, in turn.
Read a lecturer's annotated reading list for an essay and decide which sources to start with, using the notes on scope, viewpoint, date and difficulty.
Combine and compare what several sources say before giving your own view: While the first study claims..., the second..., Taken together, they suggest..., Neither source addresses...

entries.workingTitle: Reading four academics on one question
entries.intent: Read four short texts by academics on whether arts subjects should be compulsory at school and find where each writer agrees or disagrees with the others.
Use the different senses of about twelve common words (polysemy): run a business, settle a bill, the latest issue, a public figure, a sound argument, a field of study.
Comment on situations and outcomes with about twelve idioms: the last straw, a blessing in disguise, the tip of the iceberg, a drop in the ocean, a long shot, a vicious circle.
Read a short story from the 1800s and follow its plot and characters through older vocabulary, long sentences and formal dialogue.
